contents.text: The U.S. had strong political and economic ties with the Allied powers, particularly the United Kingdom. Many expected that these ties, along with a desire to play a greater role on the world stage, would persuade the U.S. to immediately join the war. Read an excerpt from President Woodrow Wilson's statement to Congress in 1914. Then answer the question.

textContent.text: The people of the United States are drawn from many nations, and chiefly from the nations now at war.…Some will wish one nation, others another, to succeed in the momentous struggle. It will be easy to excite passion and difficult to allay it. Those [U.S. citizens]…whose love of their country and whose loyalty to its government should unite them…may be divided in camps of hostile opinion.…

Such divisions amongst us would be fatal to our peace of mind and might seriously stand in the way of the proper performance of our duty as the one great nation at peace, the one people holding itself ready to play a part of impartial mediation and speak the counsels of peace and accommodation, not as a partisan, but as a friend.
…The United States must be neutral in fact, as well as in name, during these days that are to try men's souls. We must be impartial in thought, as well as action.

meaning.text: working with both sides to help end a conflict

, or limiting, the food they used. Read the passage about food rationing in the United States during World War I. Then answer the question below.

textContent.text: On August 10, 1917, the government set up the U.S. Food Administration to track food supplies and help distribute them to people fighting in the war. President Wilson appointed Herbert Hoover to lead these efforts.

Hoover created programs that called on citizens to ration their food intake, ensuring more supplies could be sent to soldiers in Europe. These programs used colorful posters to educate people and encourage them to eat less meat, wheat, fats, and sugar. Slogans such as "Food will win the war" urged people to avoid wasting groceries. People were advised to eat fresh fruit and vegetables so that nonperishable dry goods could be sent overseas. Promotions for "Meatless Tuesdays" and "Wheatless Wednesdays" reminded Americans to try to avoid certain types of food.

As a result of these efforts, the U.S. Food Administration was able to double food shipments to Europe within a year. Even after the war ended, Hoover continued to organize food shipments to millions of people who were starving in central Europe.

, or limiting, the food they used. Read the passage about food rationing in the United States during World War I. Then follow the instructions below.

textContent.text: On August 10, 1917, the government set up the U.S. Food Administration to track food supplies and help distribute them to people fighting in the war. President Wilson appointed Herbert Hoover to lead these efforts.

Hoover created programs that called on citizens to ration their food intake, ensuring more supplies could be sent to soldiers in Europe. These programs used colorful posters to educate people and encourage them to eat less meat, wheat, fats, and sugar. Slogans such as "Food will win the war" urged people to avoid wasting groceries. People were advised to eat fresh fruit and vegetables so that nonperishable dry goods could be sent overseas. Promotions for "Meatless Tuesdays" and "Wheatless Wednesdays" reminded Americans to try to avoid certain types of food.

As a result of these efforts, the U.S. Food Administration was able to double food shipments to Europe within a year. Even after the war ended, Hoover continued to organize food shipments to millions of people who were starving in central Europe.

textContent.text: On August 10, 1917, the government set up the U.S. Food Administration to track food supplies and help distribute them to people fighting in the war. President Wilson appointed Herbert Hoover to lead these efforts.

Hoover created programs that called on citizens to ration their food intake, ensuring more supplies could be sent to soldiers in Europe. These programs used colorful posters to educate people and encourage them to eat less meat, wheat, fats, and sugar. Slogans such as "Food will win the war" urged people to avoid wasting groceries. People were advised to eat fresh fruit and vegetables so that nonperishable dry goods could be sent overseas. Promotions for "Meatless Tuesdays" and "Wheatless Wednesdays" reminded Americans to try to avoid certain types of food.

As a result of these efforts, the U.S. Food Administration was able to double food shipments to Europe within a year. Even after the war ended, Hoover continued to organize food shipments to millions of people who were starving in central Europe.

, or limiting, the food they used. Read the passage about food rationing in the United States during World War I. Then follow the instructions below.

textContent.text: On August 10, 1917, the government set up the U.S. Food Administration to track food supplies and help distribute them to people fighting in the war. President Wilson appointed Herbert Hoover to lead these efforts.

Hoover created programs that called on citizens to ration their food intake, ensuring more supplies could be sent to soldiers in Europe. These programs used colorful posters to educate people and encourage them to eat less meat, wheat, fats, and sugar. Slogans such as "Food will win the war" urged people to avoid wasting groceries. People were advised to eat fresh fruit and vegetables so that nonperishable dry goods could be sent overseas. Promotions for "Meatless Tuesdays" and "Wheatless Wednesdays" reminded Americans to try to avoid certain types of food.

As a result of these efforts, the U.S. Food Administration was able to double food shipments to Europe within a year. Even after the war ended, Hoover continued to organize food shipments to millions of people who were starving in central Europe.

contents.text: In early 1917, before the United States entered the war, President Wilson described in a speech to Congress his vision for postwar peace. Since the U.S. had not been involved in European conflicts of the 1800s and 1900s, Wilson believed it could play a fair and neutral role in creating a peaceful world. Read the excerpts from the speech. Then answer the question below.

textContent.text: It is inconceivable that the people of the United States should play no part in that great enterprise [of making a peaceful world].…[They should] add their authority and their power to the authority and force of other nations to guarantee peace and justice throughout the world.…

Is the present war a struggle for a just and secure peace, or only for a new balance of power?…First of all, [it] must be a peace without victory.…Victory would mean peace forced upon the loser, a victor's terms imposed upon the vanquished.…Only a peace between equals can last.…

And there is a deeper thing involved than even equality of right among organized nations. No peace can last, or ought to last, which does not recognize and accept the principle that governments derive all their just powers from the consent of the governed, and that no right anywhere exists to hand peoples about from [nation to nation] as if they were property.

contents.text: In early 1917, before the United States entered the war, President Wilson described in a speech to Congress his vision for postwar peace. Since the U.S. had not been involved in European conflicts of the 1800s and 1900s, Wilson believed it could play a fair and neutral role in creating a peaceful world. Read the excerpts from the speech. Then answer the question below.

textContent.text: It is inconceivable that the people of the United States should play no part in that great enterprise [of making a peaceful world].…[They should] add their authority and their power to the authority and force of other nations to guarantee peace and justice throughout the world.…

Is the present war a struggle for a just and secure peace, or only for a new balance of power?…First of all, [it] must be a peace without victory.…Victory would mean peace forced upon the loser, a victor's terms imposed upon the vanquished.…Only a peace between equals can last.…

And there is a deeper thing involved than even equality of right among organized nations. No peace can last, or ought to last, which does not recognize and accept the principle that governments derive all their just powers from the consent of the governed, and that no right anywhere exists to hand peoples about from [nation to nation] as if they were property.

contents.text: In early 1917, before the United States entered the war, President Wilson described in a speech to Congress his vision for postwar peace. Since the U.S. had not been involved in European conflicts of the 1800s and 1900s, Wilson believed it could play a fair and neutral role in creating a peaceful world. Read the excerpts from the speech. Then answer the question below.

textContent.text: It is inconceivable that the people of the United States should play no part in that great enterprise [of making a peaceful world].…[They should] add their authority and their power to the authority and force of other nations to guarantee peace and justice throughout the world.…

Is the present war a struggle for a just and secure peace, or only for a new balance of power?…First of all, [it] must be a peace without victory.…Victory would mean peace forced upon the loser, a victor's terms imposed upon the vanquished.…Only a peace between equals can last.…

And there is a deeper thing involved than even equality of right among organized nations. No peace can last, or ought to last, which does not recognize and accept the principle that governments derive all their just powers from the consent of the governed, and that no right anywhere exists to hand peoples about from [nation to nation] as if they were property.
